name: Priya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Nothing you say is tied to your name, so you can give me the public version and the private one. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Metro Fresh, a big supermarket in the city centre, mostly the afternoon and evening shifts. I supervise the self-checkout bay with six machines, and I also cover the staffed tills when the queue hits the door. Students, office workers and tourists, so it's a different crowd every hour, and I love that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of the shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Around 5:30, when the commuters arrive and three machines freeze at once. I'm the person with the override key and the calm voice. Then someone's trying to buy wine without ID, someone's crying about a lost card, and I'm doing all of it with sore feet and a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful but overhyped: it helps me write a shift handover or sort out a spreadsheet, and that's about it. To friends I'd say people expecting a miracle will be disappointed. Online I'd probably post that the interesting stuff is boring, like better forms and fewer typos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say it changes less than people fear, and I'd carry on. But I still live in a three-person flat share, I earn little for what I do, and I have about three weeks of savings. If my hours dip I'm in trouble, and a plateau doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use AI for my own projects: I resell second-hand clothes online and AI writes my listings, which saves about an hour a night. I'd put the extra 120 a month into savings. I'd also keep an eye out for a supervisor job at a bigger store where the pay is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I'm good at what I do, but I want it to lead to something. If nothing changes, I'm still on the same wage in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What for, at work or outside it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I made 90 last month from the resale, and that paid my share of the electric bill. It isn't much, but it's the first money that's mine and not the shop's. I won't make it a full job, only a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money pinch even if AI is a bust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame the way pay is set, not people. Supermarkets run on tiny margins and push it down to us. I'd vote for a higher minimum wage and for rules that stop cutting hours with a day's notice.

say: AI is **useful but overhyped**, and people expecting a miracle will be disappointed.
The interesting stuff is **boring**, like better forms.
think: It changes less than people fear, but my money is still **thin**, with about three weeks saved.
do: Use AI to write my **resale** listings and save about an hour a night.
Put an extra **120 a month** into savings.
Watch for a **supervisor** job at a bigger store.
feel: **Restless**: good at the job but wanting it to lead somewhere.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm still on the same wage in five years.
fieldNote: Already a **daily AI user** and runs her own side income, which keeps fear low.
The unease comes from **pay and savings**, not technology.
Wants **policy** on hours notice and minimum wage.

steps.text: Resell second-hand clothes online with AI-written listings
Put an extra 120 a month into savings
Apply for supervisor jobs at bigger stores with better pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say AI will take stock ordering, rota planning and the phone queue. The people at tills and self-checkouts feel it later. I'd tell friends that the shops that move first will cut hours first, and the staff who learn the tools will be safe a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the risk is real but not immediate. A supervisor is half people skills and half problem fixing, and the machines already do the problem fixing badly. But head office wants fewer supervisors, and I'd be a young one on a thin cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in. I'd ask my manager to let me help with the AI stock-planning pilot, take an evening data course online for about 25 a month, and move my side income up to a few hours a week. I'd pitch myself as the person who connects the floor to the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious and a bit wired. I like that there's a lot to learn and I'm not afraid of it, but I know the margin for error is small when you're a month from broke. Change is exciting when you have a net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your day would software take, and which would it never?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped test the shop's price-label app last year and found three errors in the first week. My manager wrote it up and I was told I was the reason the rollout went smoothly. Nothing in my pay changed, but I added it to my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move towards a role that joins stores to head office, like replenishment or stock analysis. It could pay 20 percent more, and it's a better bet than a till for the next ten years. I'd also look at local jobs, but there aren't many, so I'd be ready to move city.

say: AI takes **ordering and rota** first, and shops that move first cut hours first.
Staff who learn the **tools** stay safe a little longer.
think: The risk is real but not **immediate**, though head office wants fewer supervisors.
I'm young on a **thin cushion**, so a mistake costs me.
do: Ask to join the **AI stock-planning** pilot.
Take an evening **data course** for about 25 a month.
Grow my side income to a few **hours** a week.
feel: **Curious** and a bit wired, because change is exciting when you have a net.
S1.quote: I like that there's a lot to learn and I'm not afraid of it, but I know the margin for error is small when you're a month from broke.
fieldNote: She treats change as a **chance** and acts first, which suits her adaptive trait.
Her own **pilot** work gave real evidence, not just hope.
Thin savings are the **limit** on her optimism.

steps.text: Volunteer for the shop's AI stock-planning pilot
Take an evening data course for about 25 a month
Raise resale work to a few hours a week
Aim for a replenishment or stock analyst role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need public support fast: wage cover, retraining funds, even a shorter week. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now because the ones who can work with AI have a head start. And I'd post that we shouldn't let the gains go to a few firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. Thinking AI would take most office and planning work by 2028, and that competes with the jobs I'm training towards. Robots follow around 2031, and the tills and shelves are mine, so I'd have about three years to land somewhere safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into learning than saving: finish the data course in six months, then apply for any job that works with systems. I'd double the resale side income and sell on bigger platforms. I'd also tell my housemates early so we can plan the flat, and ask the union rep what help exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not paralysed. I'm someone who moves, and that helps, but there's no cushion under it. Two years is a sprint, and I'm already tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see the next two years going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Support that doesn't depend on a boss being generous. Retraining funds I can claim, rent help for a year and a guarantee that lost hours get paid out. I'd also want the firms that automate to pay into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk is that the jobs I'm training for go first. If AI does the analysis, being an analyst isn't safe either. So I'd mix skills: people work with technology, maybe something like store operations or training others to use the tools.

say: We need **public support** fast: wage cover, retraining funds and maybe a shorter week.
Learn the **tools** now, because those who can work with AI have a head start.
think: Thinking AI could take the **planning jobs** I'm training for by 2028.
Robots reach tills around **2031**, so I have about three years to land somewhere safe.
do: Finish the **data course** in six months and apply for systems jobs.
**Double** the resale side income on bigger platforms.
Ask the **union** rep what help exists.
feel: **Anxious** but moving, with no cushion under it, and already tired.
S2.quote: If AI does the analysis, being an analyst isn't safe either.
fieldNote: She sees that her **fallback** career is also exposed, which most cashiers don't consider.
Plans to blend **people and technology skills** rather than bet on one.
Wants support that doesn't depend on an **employer's** generosity.

steps.text: Finish the data course in six months
Double resale income by selling on bigger platforms
Ask the union rep what help exists for lost hours
Apply for store operations jobs that work with systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to do it right, so retraining funds should start now. I'd tell friends to get used to the tools and build a second skill. I'd also be saying we need guarantees, not good intentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pressure but also possibility. By 2031 the thinking AI is here, and by 2034 the robots reach the shop floor, when I'm 32. There's time to build a different career, and I'd rather be early than last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through a two-year part-time course in supply chain or operations, with employer help if I can get it. I'd keep the resale going and save 150 a month. I'd also volunteer to train colleagues on AI tools, which is something I'd list on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fairly steady. I'm not waiting for permission, which helps. I still get a bit of a knot thinking about 2034, when I'm 32 and the till row is mostly empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training my colleagues. I'd run short lunch sessions on how to use the free tools and build a reputation as the person who helps. It's cheap and it sets me up for a different role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try that you would not try in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with my parents and my housemates and make a proper plan, with a number: how many months of savings before I take a risk. It sounds boring, but it calms me. I like numbers when they're on my side.

say: Five years is enough to do it **right**, so retraining funds should start now.
think: There's pressure but also **possibility**, and I'd rather be early than last.
By 2034 I'm **32**, with time to build a different career.
do: Study a two-year part-time **supply chain** course.
Save **150 a month** and keep the resale going.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, with a knot about 2034 and an empty till row.
S3.quote: I'd rather be early than last.
fieldNote: The extra time makes her **proactive** and community-minded.
She sets a **number** for risk: months of savings before she jumps.
Teaching colleagues is both **kind** and career strategy.

steps.text: Start a two-year part-time supply chain course
Save 150 a month toward six months of expenses
Run short lunch sessions for colleagues on free AI tools
Keep the resale shop going alongside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's plenty of time, but only if people use it. I'd tell friends to treat the next ten years as a chance to build something, not a countdown. I'd still push for fair rules on who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly good, with a worry. By 2036 I'm 37 and could be in a better job, but pay is thin now, and the risk of a long delay is I never leave the tills. The fix is to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, then move into a supply chain or operations role by about 2030. I'd save for a deposit and probably switch city if the best job is elsewhere. And I'd keep learning the newest AI tools, because they change every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, but not carefree. I still have a thin cushion and low pay, so my mind goes to the next rent, not the next decade. Ten years gives me room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my 20-year-old self: save a month's pay before buying a pair of trainers. Be curious, because that's what has helped me most. And don't ask for permission to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger version of yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a good life with enough room for my family and my own flat. Not a fancy job, just stable and interesting. A decade is long enough to get that, if I keep moving.

say: Ten years is plenty of time, but only if people **use it**.
Treat it as a chance to **build**, not a countdown.
think: I feel mostly good, with a worry that I **never leave** the tills.
By 2036 I'm 37 and could be in a **better job** if I start now.
do: Finish the course and move into an **operations** role by about 2030.
Save for a **deposit** and switch city if the best job is elsewhere.
Keep learning each year's new **AI tools**.
feel: Fairly **calm**, though my mind goes to the next rent, not the next decade.
S4.quote: Be curious, because that's what has helped me most. And don't ask for permission to learn.
fieldNote: Mood stays **uneasy** because rent and thin savings dominate, not AI.
Her **curiosity** and early use of tools are her main assets.
Goal is a **stable** life, not status.

steps.text: Finish the course and move into an operations role by 2030
Switch city if the best operations job is elsewhere
Learn each year's new AI tools as they come out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there isn't a net under me yet. What would help is retraining money I can actually claim, rent help for a year, and employers that train staff before they replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People assume cashiers aren't curious about this. We see the technology before most offices do. If you want to know how a new system really works, ask the person with the override key.

headlineQuote: If you want to know how a new system really works, ask the person with the override key.
portrait: Priya is 27, a **supervisor** at a busy city-centre supermarket, strong at her job but on lower pay.
She shares a flat, has about **three weeks** of savings and few similar jobs nearby.
She uses AI every day, resells clothes online, and treats change as a **chance** to move.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there is no safety net under her yet.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** she can claim, a year of rent help, and employers who train before replacing.
